mcqs.question: Why does Store depend on ExpiryPolicy and PersistenceStrategy as interfaces rather than concrete implementations?
options: So that get() and set() can run without a hashmap
Because concrete classes cannot be stored as fields in most languages
Because Entry objects require an interface to hold a value and an expiry timestamp
So expiry behavior and persistence behavior can each be swapped independently without changing Store's core get/set/delete logic
mcqs.explanation: Depending on interfaces is what makes the design extensible — a new persistence strategy or expiry approach plugs in without touching Store. Concrete classes are perfectly storable as fields; Entry doesn't need an interface to hold two fields; and Store still relies on a hashmap internally regardless of how expiry or persistence are implemented.

mcqs.question: Why is lazy expiry alone not sufficient to bound the memory used by expired keys?
options: Lazy expiry cannot coexist with a hashmap-based Store
Lazy expiry only works for keys with a TTL under one second
Lazy expiry requires scanning the entire map on every get(), which is too slow
A key that expires and is never accessed again is never checked, so it stays in memory indefinitely unless something else removes it
mcqs.explanation: Lazy expiry only fires when a key is actually accessed — a key nobody touches again after expiring simply sits in memory forever under lazy expiry alone, which is why an active sweep is needed alongside it. Lazy expiry works for any TTL duration, checks only the single key being accessed (not the whole map), and works fine with a plain hashmap.

mcqs.question: When would a min-heap of expiry times be worth its extra implementation complexity over lazy expiry plus active sweep?
options: Never — active sweep always dominates a min-heap for any workload
Only when the store has fewer than 100 keys
When precise, immediate expiry matters — such as a session store where a stale session must vanish exactly on time, rather than within a bounded sweep interval
When TTLs are not used at all
mcqs.explanation: A min-heap always knows the next key to expire, giving immediate, precise removal — worth the extra bookkeeping when exact timing matters, like invalidating a session the instant it's stale. It isn't strictly dominant over active sweep (which is simpler and sufficient for most workloads), its value doesn't depend on total key count, and it's irrelevant if TTLs aren't used at all since there'd be nothing to schedule.

mcqs.question: The active expiry sweep runs on a background thread while other threads call get()/set() concurrently on the same map. What's the concurrency risk if this isn't handled carefully?
options: The sweep thread removing a key while another thread is mid-lookup on it is a data race unless mutation and iteration are properly synchronized
Background threads cannot access the same hashmap as the main thread in any language
The risk only exists if TTLs are longer than the sweep interval
There is no risk as long as the sweep runs less than once per second
mcqs.explanation: Two threads touching the same mutable map concurrently — one deleting, one reading — is the classic concurrent-mutation hazard regardless of TTL duration or sweep frequency; it needs a lock fine-grained enough to avoid serializing every read, or a concurrent-safe map. Background threads absolutely can share a map with the main thread in virtually every mainstream language; the danger is purely about unsynchronized concurrent mutation.

mcqs.question: Why is writing to disk synchronously on every set() call a poor default for an in-memory key-value store?
options: It couples the store's in-memory speed to disk I/O latency on every mutation, defeating the store's core purpose of fast reads and writes
Disk writes cannot be performed from within a set() method
It makes TTL expiry stop working correctly
It only affects get() calls, not set() calls
mcqs.explanation: The whole value proposition of an in-memory store is speed; forcing every mutation to wait on disk I/O erodes exactly that. Disk writes are perfectly callable from set(); TTL expiry is unrelated to persistence timing; and the described cost falls on set() specifically, not get().
